title: S7 — MEP Fundamentals for the Non-MEP Manager

concepts.title: Slope is sacred
concepts.mechanism: Drain and waste piping relies entirely on gravity — there is no pump making wastewater flow, only a continuous downhill slope from fixture to sewer connection. Even a short flat or back-pitched section anywhere along that run creates a low point where waste and water sit instead of flowing through, leading to standing water, odors, and clogs. A tight ceiling space that seems to force a flat run isn't actually optional to accept — the pipe has to reroute, or the ceiling has to change, because gravity itself does not negotiate.
concepts.mechanismPro: Maintain minimum slope (commonly around 1/4 in per foot for smaller drain lines) continuously from fixture to connection; any apparent ceiling-height conflict is a coordination problem to solve in design, not a slope to compromise in the field.
concepts.hook: A marble rolled along a mostly-downhill track with one flat dip in the middle stops right there, in the dip, no matter how steep the rest of the track is. One flat section undoes the whole slope.

applied.prompt: A condo's ceiling space is too tight to maintain drain slope in one section without dropping the ceiling further, which the architect resists. What do you require?

options.label: Hold the drainage slope and force the ceiling/routing coordination to solve around it
options.outcome: Right. Slope is not a design preference to trade away — a flat section becomes a standing-water and clog problem the day the building is occupied.

options.label: Reroute the drain line entirely to a path with adequate headroom, even if longer
options.outcome: A legitimate fix that preserves the physics — often the actual right answer when the direct path genuinely can't carry the slope.

options.label: Accept a flat section to preserve the architect's ceiling height
options.outcome: This creates a permanent low point where solids settle and water sits — a maintenance and odor problem baked into the building for its entire life, to save a few inches of ceiling in one hallway.

applied.debrief: This is the same drainage law as M01's site-wide groundwater management, at building scale: water always wins unless you give it a planned way out, and a plan that skips slope 'just this once' isn't actually a plan.

concepts.title: Everything cold sweats: sizing AC for water, not just heat
concepts.mechanism: In humid Bahamian air, ANY surface below the dew point — an uninsulated duct, a chilled pipe, even an over-cooled ceiling tile — grows liquid water out of thin air, the same way a cold drink sweats on a porch. An air conditioner only pulls humidity out of the air while it's actually running. An oversized unit blasts the room down to temperature in minutes and shuts off, long before it has wrung much water out of the air at all. The result is a cold, clammy room stuck at high humidity, where every cool surface keeps sweating and mold farms itself quietly behind the scenes. A right-sized unit runs longer and gentler, and spends that runtime doing its real tropical job: removing water, with cooling as the side effect.
concepts.mechanismPro: Size cooling equipment to Manual-J load calculations that account for latent (moisture) load, not just sensible heat, since short-cycling from oversizing fails to dehumidify even as it satisfies the thermostat; insulate any duct or pipe surface that can fall below the space dew point, since bare metal at supply-air temperature is a guaranteed condensation source in this climate.
concepts.hook: Wringing a wet towel: a huge machine that squeezes it for two seconds leaves it cold but still dripping. A smaller machine that squeezes steadily for ten minutes hands you a dry towel. Runtime is what wrings the water out — of a towel, or of a room.

applied.prompt: Condo buyers' agents push for 'more powerful' AC as a selling point, and the mechanical sub offers a discount on units one size up across all 108 condos; separately, a value-engineering line proposes deleting insulation on condensate-adjacent duct runs above bathroom ceilings.

options.label: Hold Manual-J-appropriate sizing and keep duct insulation, and give sales a better story: 'engineered for tropical humidity'
options.outcome: Right. This is the actual tropical-climate answer — a unit sized to run long enough to dehumidify, with no cold surfaces left exposed to sweat.

options.label: Accept the larger units but keep the duct insulation
options.outcome: Removes one failure mode but not the other — short-cycling still leaves indoor humidity high even though nothing is visibly sweating yet.

options.label: Accept the larger units and delete the duct insulation to save cost
options.outcome: Short-cycling keeps humidity around 70% while bare, cold ducts sweat directly onto ceiling drywall above bathrooms — the marina-view condos develop a mildew smell within two years of occupancy.

applied.debrief: Same law, new disguise as V3-5's wall assembly: v35's poly sheet and this duct are the identical failure — a surface below dew point sitting in humid air. One hides inside a wall, the other drips onto a ceiling tile; once you can ask 'is anything here colder than the dew point,' you'll spot both.

summary: Enough plumbing, electrical, and HVAC to manage the trades: drainage slope is sacred, the corrosion tax on coastal electrical is real, and tropical HVAC is dehumidification first — oversized AC makes mold. Plus the coordination discipline that is the actual CM skill. PLAIN: water flows downhill, salt eats metal, cold surfaces sweat. PRO: quarter-inch per foot, coastal-rated equipment, Manual-J right-sizing.

sections.heading: Plumbing: pressure up, gravity down
sections.body: PLAIN: Supply water is pushed (pressure); waste water only falls (gravity) — and its slope is sacred: too flat and solids strand, and a flat or back-graded drain cast INTO a slab is jackhammer work to fix. That's why the slab plumbing gets surveyed before every pour. PRO: 1/4 in per ft standard for small drains; slab rough-in survey is a mandatory hold point; vents protect trap seals (sewer-gas complaints = venting defects); pressure math for the condos: ~0.43 psi lost per foot of elevation plus friction — upper floors may need booster pumps off WSC pressure. Community scale: gravity mains → lift stations → the package WWTP; grease interceptors at every food outlet (clubhouse, sports bar, beach club) or the WWTP dies young.

sections.heading: Electrical: sizing and the corrosion tax
sections.body: PLAIN: Houses need 150–200A services; condo buildings need real load calculations and meter banks. And the sea eats electrical equipment — panels, AC condensers, fixtures — anything standard-grade within the salt zone gets replaced in 5–7 years. PRO: coastal-rated equipment (coated-coil condensers, stainless/NEMA-appropriate enclosures) at a 15–35% premium, or budget the replacement wave; standby power is near-mandatory at community scale — a lift station without backup power overflows sewage in the first long outage; community generator $250–800K; solar-ready conduit is cheap now and expensive later.

sections.heading: HVAC: dehumidification first, and the coordination discipline
sections.body: PLAIN: In the tropics, air conditioning's real job is wringing water out of the air. An OVERSIZED unit cools the room so fast it shuts off before dehumidifying — cold, clammy, and eventually moldy. Bigger is not better; calculated is better. PRO: Manual-J-type load calc, right-size (~1 ton per 450–600 sf here, calc governs), ducts in conditioned/sealed space, fresh-air strategy that doesn't import humidity, condensate disposal designed (every unit drips constantly). Mold is the #1 tropical warranty class and is designed out, not cleaned out. The actual CM skill is COORDINATION: coordinated shop drawings before frame pours (M7 stacking), sleeve/embed drawings to the concrete crew, rough-in inspections at every close-up, and commissioning for the commercial buildings — fire alarm/sprinkler acceptance, kitchen hoods, WWTP process proving — with the authorities booked weeks ahead.

quiz.teach: The slab pour will bury the drainage piping forever — the survey is the last look.
quiz.prompt: The pre-pour survey shows one bathroom group 40 ft from the stack at dead-flat grade. The pour is scheduled for 6 AM. Stop it?

choices.text: Yes — a flat drain cast into concrete strands solids for the life of the house, and the fix is a jackhammer; a day's pour delay is the cheapest this problem will ever be
choices.why: Correct. At 1/4 in/ft, 40 ft needs 10 inches of fall; dead-flat means the line never worked. The pour is the point of no return.
Water maybe; solids strand at zero slope, forever. 'It'll probably drain' is a warranty claim with a schedule.

choices.text: Pour, and increase the fixture flow to compensate
choices.why: Flow doesn't create fall. The physics is elevation, and after 6 AM the elevation is permanent.

choices.text: Pour around that bathroom and fix it later
choices.why: A blockout is actually a legitimate variant of stopping — but only as a planned, formed blockout, not an improvised gap in a structural slab at 5:45 AM.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: drains only work downhill, and after the pour the hill is cast in stone. PRO: 'quarter-inch per foot, surveyed before every pour, hold point — no sign-off, no concrete.' This is why the slab rough-in survey sits on the mandatory list. (S7)

quiz.teach: AC removes moisture only while it's running — a unit that cycles off quickly barely dehumidifies.
quiz.prompt: Explain the oversized-AC-makes-mold mechanism (the one behind the sim's Phase 7 warranty cluster).

choices.text: The oversized unit hits the thermostat's temperature fast and shuts off before pulling meaningful moisture — the space is cold but humid, surfaces drop below the air's dew point, condensation feeds mold
choices.why: Correct. Short-cycling is the term: cooling capacity outran the dehumidification time. Cold + humid = condensing surfaces = mold farm.
Leakage is a maintenance issue unrelated to sizing. The mechanism is runtime: moisture removal needs the coil cold and the air moving across it for TIME.
Duct condensation is real (uninsulated ducts in hot attics) but it's a different defect — the sizing mechanism is short-cycling.

choices.text: It doesn't — more cooling is more drying
choices.why: The seductive intuition that builds moldy houses. Drying is a function of runtime, and oversizing kills runtime.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the too-big AC wins the temperature race and quits before finishing the moisture job — like a dishwasher that stops after the rinse. PRO: 'Manual-J load calc, right-size, design for latent load; mold is designed out, not cleaned out.' (S7, V3-9)

quiz.teach: Lift stations pump sewage uphill — with electricity.
quiz.prompt: Why is backup power for the lift stations described as near-mandatory rather than optional resilience?

choices.text: A lift station without power doesn't pause — it overflows raw sewage in the first long outage, into your canals and streets, on an island grid where long outages are a design condition
choices.why: Correct. The wet well keeps filling whether the pumps run or not. The failure mode isn't inconvenience; it's an environmental incident with your marina attached.

choices.text: Buyers expect generators at this price point
choices.why: Standby power IS a sales feature — but the lift stations would need it in a community of saints. Sewage physics doesn't care about the market segment.
The utility cares about your connection, not your wet wells. This requirement comes from consequence analysis, not the interconnection agreement.

choices.text: It's only needed during hurricane season
choices.why: Grid outages here aren't seasonal — and the wet well fills at dinner time year-round.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the sewage pump that stops doesn't wait — it overflows. PRO: 'auto-transfer standby at every lift station, or one community plant with ATS — designed in, exercised monthly.' Failure lands in YOUR canal, upstream of YOUR estate lots. (S7, M12 risk #9)

quiz.teach: Commissioning is the proving phase: systems demonstrated working, witnessed by authorities.
quiz.prompt: Why do commissioning authorities get booked weeks ahead instead of when the building is 'ready'?

choices.text: Because inspector calendars are queues, and fire alarm/sprinkler acceptance gates the OC — booking backward from their available dates is schedule design; booking at 'ready' adds their backlog to your OC date
choices.why: Correct. The commissioning sequence (alarm → sprinkler → hoods → elevators) has dependencies AND external calendars — plan around both or the finished building waits on a diary.
Authorities don't discount; they schedule. The value of early booking is CALENDAR position, which converts directly to OC date.

choices.text: It's a courtesy that builds relationships
choices.why: Relationships help (Module 13), but the mechanism is queueing math: their backlog becomes your revenue delay unless you're already in the book.

choices.text: Commissioning can run before construction completes anyway
choices.why: Some pre-testing can; ACCEPTANCE tests need finished systems — which is why the finish schedule gets built backward from the booked dates.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the inspector's diary is part of your schedule — get in it early. PRO: 'book AHJs weeks out, sequence completion backward from acceptance dates.' The sim's elevator-backlog and fuel-commissioning events are this lesson wearing different hats. (S7, M7)

mathProblems.title: Tonnage for a house
mathProblems.context: Right-sizing math: conditioned area ÷ sf-per-ton (climate-adjusted; the load calc governs, but this is the sanity check). Round up to the unit size.

mathProblems.title: The corrosion tax, priced up front
mathProblems.context: Coastal-rated electrical and HVAC equipment carries a 15–35% premium over standard — the alternative is a year-5–7 replacement wave in occupied homes.

decisionPoints.title: Lift station backup: per-station or one plant
decisionPoints.scenario: Four lift stations serve the community. Option A: a standby generator with automatic transfer at each station (four small units, four fuel systems, four maintenance contracts). Option B: one community generator plant with automatic transfer feeding the stations plus the amenity core (bigger unit, single point of maintenance — and a single point of failure, plus distribution runs). The sales team notes 'community backup power' is a brochure line either way.

options.label: Let consequence analysis pick: stations closest to the canal get dedicated units (overflow there is an environmental incident), the rest plus amenities share the community plant — a hybrid sized by failure cost, with monthly exercised transfers
options.outcome: The hybrid puts redundancy where the consequence is worst (sewage near your marina water) and efficiency where it's tolerable. The monthly exercise log — generators that never run don't start — is the part everyone forgets and the audit remembers.

options.label: One community plant — simplest to maintain, best brochure
options.outcome: Efficient until the single point fails during the single outage it existed for — with all four stations filling at once. Defensible with rigorous maintenance and a portable-generator connection point at each station as the manual backstop.

options.label: Rough in the transfer switches, buy generators 'when the budget recovers'
options.outcome: The switches without the generators are hope with wiring. The first long outage arrives before the budget does, and the overflow report writes itself — including the line item you deferred.

decisionPoints.debrief: Backup power topology is consequence engineering: rank the failure costs (sewage to the canal > dark clubhouse), put hard redundancy at the top of the list, and exercise everything monthly — standby equipment that's never run is decoration. (S7)
